title: Dubu Jorim
subtitle: Braised spicy tofu in soy and gochugaru sauce
excerpt: Firm tofu is pan-fried until golden, then simmered in a glossy soy and gochugaru sauce until the liquid reduces and clings to every piece. It is one of the most popular everyday banchan in Korean households. Ready in under 20 minutes, it works as a side dish or a simple main over rice.
sourceNotes: Dubu jorim is a staple of Korean home cooking, appearing on tables across the country as a reliable everyday banchan. The dish reflects the Korean preference for building deep flavour through reduction rather than long cooking, with the sauce thickening naturally as it simmers down around the fried tofu.

glossaryTerms.definition: Jorim is a Korean cooking method in which ingredients are simmered in a seasoned liquid that gradually reduces until it coats the food in a thick, glossy sauce. Unlike a braise where liquid remains, jorim relies on reduction to concentrate flavour directly onto the ingredient. It is used with tofu, fish, potatoes and meat.

Dubu is the Korean word for tofu. In Korean cooking, firm dubu is the standard choice for pan-frying and braising because it holds its shape well under heat. Silken varieties are reserved for soups and softer dishes. Firm dubu should be pressed briefly before cooking to remove excess moisture.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 as a side dish and takes around 20 minutes from start to finish.
gets its character from the two-stage process: pan-frying the
first to create a lightly crisp surface, then braising it in a punchy soy and gochugaru sauce that clings as it reduces.

Press the tofu for at least 5 minutes before cooking. Lay the block on a clean tea towel, place a heavy plate on top, and let the weight draw out moisture. Dry tofu browns quickly in the pan and absorbs the braising sauce far more effectively than wet tofu does.

items.prepNote: cut into 1cm slabs, pressed and dried

content.text: Press and dry the tofu, then cut into slabs roughly 1cm thick. Pat each piece dry with kitchen paper.
Heat the neutral oil in a wide frying pan over a medium-high heat. Add the tofu in a single layer and cook for 3 to 4 minutes per side until golden. Remove and set aside.
In a small bowl, stir together the soy sauce, gochugaru, sugar, garlic, and water to make the braising sauce.
Return the pan to a medium heat. Add the white parts of the spring onions and cook for 30 seconds, then pour in the braising sauce.
Nestle the fried tofu into the sauce. Simmer for 5 to 7 minutes, spooning the sauce over the tofu as it reduces, until the liquid is thick and glossy and coats the pieces.
Remove from the heat. Drizzle with sesame oil, scatter over the green spring onion tops and sesame seeds, and serve immediately.

items.symptom: Tofu sticks to the pan and tears when flipping
items.cause: The tofu was too wet or the pan was not hot enough before adding the oil
items.fix: Press the tofu thoroughly and make sure the oil is shimmering before adding the pieces. Do not move them until a crust has formed underneath, around 3 to 4 minutes.

items.cause: The heat was too high and the liquid boiled off too fast
items.fix: Keep the heat at medium rather than high once the tofu goes back in. The sauce should bubble gently, not boil aggressively.

items.symptom: Dish tastes flat and not spicy enough
items.cause: Gochugaru heat levels vary by brand
items.fix: Taste the sauce before adding the tofu and adjust the gochugaru or add a small splash more soy sauce. Different brands range from mild to quite fiery.

content.text: Dubu jorim appears on Korean tables as a banchan alongside rice and soup. It is economical and quick. Most families have their own version, some milder and some much hotter. Leftovers keep in the fridge for two days and taste even better the next day once the sauce has soaked further into the tofu.
